passages.name: Dare

passages.text:
Tell me more 

[[Being trans in prison means you don’t just do time — you get studied.

At intake, they ask the questions. Are you transgender? Have you been assaulted before? Do you think you’re at risk? You can feel the room shift when you answer. From that point on, you’re not just a person — you’re a category.

In population, you’re always aware of yourself. How you walk. How you talk. Who’s watching. Some people leave you alone. Some don’t. Staff might use the wrong name like it’s nothing. Medical care turns into paperwork and waiting and hoping someone believes you.

If they decide you’re “too vulnerable,” they move you for “protection.” That usually means isolation. A locked door is still a locked door, even if they say it’s for your own good.

You learn to calculate everything. Who’s safe. When to correct someone. When to let it go. You get good at shrinking, or at standing still.

Mostly, it’s exhausting.
Trying to survive.
Trying not to disappear.]]
passages.name: Didn't fight. Didn't break a rule. Didn't even raise my voice. Just failed their little math problem about bodies and boxes.
Hmm okay, challenge accepted, I guess

passages.text:
Sneak a peek?
That’s kind of the point — you’re not really supposed to own it in here.

Yeah, it’s supposed to be accessible when we ask. That’s what they say. But ‘accessible’ usually means there’s one copy somewhere in the unit office. Or on a cart. Or ‘I’ll bring it next round.’

In SHU, you don’t just walk to a shelf. You request it. You wait. If the officer’s busy, short-staffed, or just not in the mood, it doesn’t happen. And if you ask again too soon, now you’re being pushy.

Even when they do bring it, you get a few minutes standing at the door, trying to skim policies written in legal language that references three other policies you don’t have.

So yeah — it should be accessible, but it's still a challenge.

[[Challenge accepted, I guess]]

passages.name: Truth

passages.text:
What good can it do?

It’s not about the fancy words.

It’s about knowing what they’re supposed to do versus what they’re actually doing.

The guidebook lays out timelines. Reviews. Access to property. How long you can be in here before someone has to look at your case again. How to file a grievance. What counts as ‘protective custody’ and what they owe you while you’re in it.

Without it, everything feels arbitrary. Like whatever happens to you just… happens.

With it, at least you can say, ‘No, that’s not what your policy says.’

It doesn’t fix the system. It doesn’t open the door.

But it gives you something solid to stand on in a place where most of the ground keeps shifting.

[[Hmm okay, challenge accepted, I guess]]
